		  <command>nbd-server</command> will try to open
		  <filename>/export/192.168.0.0/192.168.1.100</filename>;

		  <constant>cidrhash 26</constant>, then
		  <command>nbd-server</command> will try to open
		  <filename>/export/192.168.1.64/192.168.1.100</filename>.
		</para>
		<para>For IPv6, in the above example, with
		<constant>cidrhash 42</constant>, the filename would
		be
		<filename>/export/2001:32f:6c0:0:0:0:0:0/2001:32f:6f8:0:0:0:0:39</filename>.</para>
	      </listitem>
	    </varlistentry>
	  </variablelist>
	</listitem>
      </varlistentry>
      <varlistentry>
        <term><option>tlsonly</option></term>
	<listitem>
	  <para>Optional; boolean.</para>
	  <para>When this option is enabled,
	    <command>nbd-server</command> will only serve the export
	    using the TLS extension. If this option is not supplied,
	    TLS is optional, unless <option>tlsonly</option> is set
            in the generic section. In order for TLS to work at all,
            the <option>keyfile</option> option must be specified in
            the generic section.
	  </para>
	</listitem>
      </varlistentry>
      <varlistentry>
        <term><option>waitfile</option></term>
	<listitem>
	  <para>Optional; string.</para>
	  <para>When this option is set, <command>nbd-server</command>
	    will allow writes to this export, but not reads, until the
	    server is sent a SIGUSR1 command. Any writes to the export
	    will be stored in a diff file with the same algorithm as for
	    the copy-on-write option. In particular, this means that the
	    <option>cowdir</option> option is in effect for this option,
	    too.</para>
	  <para>The backend file (as per the exportname parameter) need
	    not exist until the SIGUSR1 signal is sent to the
	    server.</para>

	    will open the main export file, and start merging all
	    outstanding writes into it. Once this operation finishes,
	    the diff file will be removed, and the server will allow
	    normal use of the export.</para>

	    from one server to another.</para>
	  <para>Note that this option cannot be combined with the
	    copy-on-write option itself.</para>

This is extremely helpful. This man page describes the full upstream semantics:

1. `copyonwrite`: writes don't go to the master file; they go to a separate file that is deleted on disconnect. Reads after a write return the written data.
2. `cowdir`: where to write CoW diff files; if absent, same directory as the base export file.
3. `sparse_cow`: use a sparse file for CoW (same size as the export); when disabled, each newly-written block is mapped to the end of the CoW file, and lseek is needed per 4096-byte block.
4. `waitfile` (F_WAIT): allow writes but not reads until SIGUSR1; writes are saved to a diff file using the same algorithm as CoW; cowdir applies; when SIGUSR1 arrives, open the main export file, merge the outstanding writes, delete the diff file, and allow normal use. Cannot be combined with copyonwrite (the parse-time check already exists).

Note: in this codebase, F_WAIT is parsed as `waitfile` and is treated as PARAM_BOOL. Hmm, wait — in the code it's `{ "waitfile", FALSE, PARAM_BOOL, &(s.flags), F_WAIT }`. Upstream, waitfile is a boolean flag. OK.

Now, let me look at the test cow-client.c to understand what exactly the test is verifying.
The man page documents the full CoW semantics. Now let me look at the CoW test client, which encodes the expected behavior precisely.

The test client is very clear:

1. `init <file>`: Create a master file with a deterministic pattern.
2. `write <host> <port> <export>`: Connect, write several regions (aligned full pages, partial writes spanning pages, multi-page unaligned writes, and rewrites of pages that have already been dirtied), then read the entire export — the written data must be visible immediately, and the rest must be the original pattern. Then disconnect.
3. `read <host> <port> <export>`: On a new connection, the export must once again show only the original pattern.
4. `checkfile <file>`: The master file on disk must contain only the original pattern (writes must not have leaked through).

  <refsect1>
    <title>DESCRIPTION</title>

    <para><command>&dhpackage;</command> is the server for the Linux
    Network Block Device (NBD). With NBD, a client can use a file,
    exported over the network from a server, as a block device. It can
    then be used for whatever purpose a normal block device (harddisk,
    CD-ROM, ...) can be used for.</para>

    <para>NBD can be useful for diskless clients that need swapspace,
    but you can also create a filesystem on it and use it as though it
    were a local filesystem.</para>

    <para><command>&dhpackage;</command> implements some security
    through a file called "@MAN_SYSCONFDIR@/nbd-server/allow" (by default; a
    different file can be chosen with the '-l' option or through a
    config file specification). This file must list the IP-addresses or
    network masks of clients that are allowed to connect. If it does not
    exist, all clients are able to connect. If the file is empty, no
    clients can connect.</para>

    <para>Note that while the command line allows for specifying an
    export, the use of this option is deprecated. It is preferred to
    make use of a configuration file instead, the format of which is
    defined in nbd-server(5).</para>

   <para>While nbd-server is running, new exports can be added by
   re-writing configuration files and then sending SIGHUP to
   nbd-server. SIGHUP causes nbd-server to re-read its configuration
   files and to start serving all new exports which were not served
   earlier. Reconfiguration does not modify any existing export, it only
   appends new ones.</para>

	<term>ip</term>

	  be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, or a hostname. In the
	  latter case, nbd-server will do a hostname lookup for the
	  name specified, and will listen on the first address that is
	  returned. For compatibility with past versions of
	  nbd-server, if an IPv4 address is specified, the @ sign that
	  serves as separator between the address and port may be
	  replaced by a colon.</para>
	  <para>If this parameter is not specified, nbd-server will
	  listen on all local addresses on both IPv4 and IPv6. To
	  limit to IPv4, specify the address as 0.0.0.0; to limit to
	  IPv6, specify it as ::.</para>
	</listitem>
      </varlistentry>
      <varlistentry>
	<term><option>port</option>

	<listitem>

	  "%s", then this %s will be substituded with the IP-address

	    m, in which case the size will be multiplied by 1024 (K
	    or k) or 1048576 (M or m)</para>
	</listitem>
      </varlistentry>
      <varlistentry>
	<term><option>-r</option></term>
	<listitem>
	  <para>Export the file read-only. If a client tries to write
	    to a read-only exported file, it will receive an error, but
	    the connection will stay up.</para>
	</listitem>
      </varlistentry>
      <varlistentry>
	<term><option>-m</option></term>
	<listitem>

	    blockdevices that are larger than the maximum allowed
	    filesize on a given filesystem; i.e. when the filesystem
	    does not allow files larger than 2GB (which is true for
	    Linux 2.2 and below), you can use this option to store the
	    data in multiple files and export a larger filesystem, if
	    needed.</para>
	  <para>

	    with names in the format "name.X", where "name" is given as
	    the filename argument to nbd-server, and "X" is a number
	    starting by 0 and going up for each file.
	  </para>
	  <para>

	    future versions.</para>
	</listitem>
      </varlistentry>

	    separate file. This separate file is removed when the
	    connection is closed, which means that serving this way will
	    make nbd-server slow down (especially on large block devices

	    warning is harmless and may be ignored.</para>
	</listitem>

        <term><option>-M</option></term>
	<listitem>

	  parameter is not specified, no limit is set.</para>
	</listitem>
      </varlistentry>
      <varlistentry>
        <term><option>-V</option></term>
	<listitem>

        </listitem>

      <varlistentry>
        <term><option>-d</option></term>
	<listitem>

	  Implies <option>-n</option>.</para>
	</listitem>
      </varlistentry>
      <varlistentry>
	<term><option>host list filename</option></term>
	<listitem>
	  <para>This argument should contain a list of IP-addresses
	    for hosts that may connect to the server. Wildcards are
	    <emphasis>not</emphasis> allowed. If the file does not
	    exist, it is ignored (and any host can connect); If the file
	    does exist, but is empty, no host can connect. By default,
	    the name 'nbd_server.allow' is used, and looked for in the
	    current directory, unless nbd-server is compiled as a
	    daemon, in which case it is looked for in the
	    root-directory.</para>
	</listitem>

	  command line, then &dhpackage; will output a configuration
	  file section with this as the header that is functionally
	  equivalent to the other options specified on the command line,
	  and exit. This is useful for migrating pre-2.9 nbd-server
	  initscript configuration files to the new format.</para>
	</listitem>

  <refsect1>
    <title>EXAMPLES</title>
    <para>Some examples of nbd-server usage:</para>
    <itemizedlist mark="none">
      <listitem>
	<para>To export a file /export/nbd/exp-bl-dev on port 2000:</para>
	<para><command>nbd-server 2000 /export/nbd/exp-bl-dev</command></para>

	<para>To export a the same file read-only:</para>

	<para>To export the same file read-write, but make sure
	  changes are lost after restarting the client or the
	  server:</para>
	<para><command>nbd-server 2000 /export/nbd/exp-bl-dev

### 1. CLIENT Struct Fields Related to Copy-on-Write
The `CLIENT` struct definition is not present in this file (it is located in `nbdsrv.h`, included via `#include <nbdsrv.h>`). However, the following fields are accessed verbatim within this file's COW logic:

*   `client->server->cowdir`

### 2. Functions Implementing Copy-on-Write or Waitfile
*   `copyonwrite_prepare(CLIENT* client)` – Initializes diff file and map.
*   `expread(READ_CTX *ctx, CLIENT *client)` – Handles reads with COW/waitfile diversion.
*   `expwrite(off_t a, char *buf, size_t len, CLIENT *client, int fua)` – Handles writes with COW/waitfile diversion.
*   `expflush(CLIENT *client)` – Flushes diff file if COW or WAIT flags are set.
*   `commit_diff(CLIENT* client, bool lock, int fhandle)` – Merges dirty pages from diff file to base file.
*   `wait_file(void *void_ptr)` – Thread function handling F_WAIT logic and SIGUSR1 merging.
*   `finalize_client(CLIENT* client)` – Unlinks diff file on disconnect if F_COPYONWRITE is set.

### 3. Diff File Naming, Creation, and Removal
*   **Naming:** Created in `copyonwrite_prepare`. Format: `<cowdir_or_export_dir>/<export_basename>-<client_name>-<pid>.diff`.
    ```c
    client->difffilename = g_strdup_printf("%s/%s-%s-%d.diff",dir,export_base,client->clientname, (int)getpid());
    ```
*   **Creation:** Opened with `O_RDWR | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC` and mode `0600` in `copyonwrite_prepare`.
    ```c
    client->difffile=open(client->difffilename,O_RDWR | O_CREAT | O_TRUNC,0600) ;
    ```
*   **Removal:** Deleted in `finalize_client` only if `F_COPYONWRITE` is active.
    ```c
    if(client->server->flags & F_COPYONWRITE) {
        unlink(client->difffilename);
    }
    ```

### 4. Read/Write Diversion Logic
Diversion occurs in `expread` and `expwrite` when `F_COPYONWRITE` is set OR when `F_WAIT` is set and `client->export == NULL`. The granularity is `DIFFPAGESIZE` (4096 bytes).

*   **Reads (`expread`):** Checks `client->difmap[page_index]`.
    *   If value is not `(uint32_t)(-1)`: Reads from `client->difffile` at offset `difmap[index] * DIFFPAGESIZE + offset`.
    *   If value is `-1`: Falls back to `rawexpread_fully` (base file), unless `F_WAIT` is active and export is NULL (returns error/fail).
*   **Writes (`expwrite`):** Checks `client->difmap[page_index]`.
    *   If mapped: Writes directly to `client->difffile`.
    *   If unmapped: Allocates a new slot in difffile. If `F_SPARSE` is set, uses page index as slot; otherwise increments `client->difffilelen`. If writing a partial page, reads the full original page from base first (`rawexpread`), merges new data, then writes full page to diff file. Updates `difmap`.

### 5. Waitfile / SIGUSR1 Merging Logic
*   **Signal Handler:** `sigusr1_handler` posts to a global semaphore `file_wait_sem`.
    ```c
    static void sigusr1_handler(const int s G_GNUC_UNUSED) {
        msg(LOG_INFO, "Got SIGUSR1");
        sem_post(&file_wait_sem);
    }
    ```
*   **Wait Thread (`wait_file`):** Spawned in `setupexport` if `F_WAIT` is set.
    1.  Blocks on `sem_wait(&file_wait_sem)` in a loop until the base file (`client->server->exportname`) can be opened successfully.
    2.  Once file appears, calls `commit_diff` repeatedly to merge dirty pages from `difffile` to the newly opened base file handle.
    3.  Takes `client->export_lock` (write lock) for final merge pass and switching `client->export` to point to the real file.
    4.  After switching, subsequent I/O bypasses COW logic because `client->export` is no longer NULL.
*   **Constraint:** Configuration parsing explicitly forbids mixing `F_COPYONWRITE` and `F_WAIT`.
